current_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether behavioral or contextual inferences about living beings (humans, animals) are biologically or physically reasonable and directly grounded in observable visual cues — but ONLY after the answer has been confirmed to be factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. If either visual grounding or factual consistency is violated, the answer is disqualified regardless of plausibility. Plausibility does not apply to non-living subjects (e.g., statues, logos, abstract art, objects), nor to spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., a giraffe in a cage). It is strictly a tiebreaker for factually consistent and visually grounded answers — not a disqualification tool or preference rule. Annotators must never use plausibility to override visual grounding, factual consistency, or to resolve ties involving factually incorrect answers. Plausibility is evaluated only for living beings or their interactions — and must be based solely on direct, unambiguous visual evidence (e.g., facial expression, posture, gaze, motion blur, physical contact). Behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’, ‘leaning forward’) are acceptable if visually supported — even if subjective — and should not be penalized. Contextually reasonable inferences (e.g., ‘serious’, ‘playful’, ‘waiting’) are valid if grounded in visual cues — not in social norms, cultural expectations, or external knowledge. Spatial or directional qualifiers (e.g., ‘toward the left’, ‘extended forward’) are allowed if visually supported — they are not hallucinations if grounded. Plausibility does not evaluate descriptive style, completeness, or specificity — only whether the inferred behavior or context is biologically or physically reasonable given the visual evidence. Annotators must reject any inference that contradicts the visual record — even if it seems ‘reasonable’ — and must avoid using plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims. The criterion must not be applied to non-living subjects — if the subject is non-living, preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency). When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative inference — and plausibility is not applicable. The goal is to reward accurate, visually grounded inferences that are contextually reasonable — and penalize only falsehoods or hallucinations — not subjective interpretations or minimalism.

current_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty_in_ambiguous_scenes
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer appropriately expresses uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly', 'appears to be', 'not clearly visible') ONLY when visual evidence is objectively ambiguous — defined as cases where the image is blurred, occluded, low-resolution, or insufficient to support definitive claims — and ONLY after the answer has been confirmed as factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. It does NOT apply to clearly visible, non-ambiguous elements — which should be described confidently without penalty — nor to hallucinations, misidentifications, or factually incorrect answers (which are disqualified under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image). Uncertainty is rewarded only when the visual record genuinely lacks clarity (e.g., partially obscured objects, indistinct textures, unresolvable spatial relationships) — not for contextually open interpretations, subjective emotional inferences (e.g., 'smiling', 'curious'), or non-literal descriptions (e.g., 'messy', 'intriguing') that are grounded in visible cues. It is not a tiebreaker — preference is determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, specificity, factual consistency) when answers are factually consistent and visually grounded. Uncertainty must not be used to mask factual errors, misrepresentations, or omissions — and must never be applied to clearly visible elements, even if non-central or contextually open. The criterion is a refinement for factually correct answers — rewarding cautious language in ambiguous visual contexts — while prioritizing visual fidelity and factual accuracy over vague or overcautious interpretations. It does NOT penalize accurate, specific descriptions of clearly visible elements — even if non-essential — nor does it penalize contextually grounded inferences (e.g., 'browsing' from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported. The goal is to reward appropriate, contextually grounded caution in ambiguous scenes — not to enforce unnecessary vagueness or penalize confident descriptions in unambiguous ones. Workers must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must never use this criterion to override or justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported claims.

current_criteria.name: completeness
current_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations (fabricated or misidentified visual elements) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically required to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly necessary to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, posture, motion, or contextually grounded actions). Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all semantically essential visual components — not all visible details, nor aesthetic descriptors, nor speculative inferences — and omission of clearly visible, semantically essential elements (e.g., posture when asked ‘what is the person doing?’) is penalized. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or contextually unsupported details (e.g., ‘a camel’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant to answering the question — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question’s literal intent. If two answers are factually consistent, the one that includes more semantically essential, visually present elements wins — but only if those elements are not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to override factual consistency — factual consistency is the non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

current_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
current_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless those elements are explicitly irrelevant to the question. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

current_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
current_criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates the internal consistency and visual fidelity of an answer’s claims — specifically, whether all stated visual elements (objects, actions, spatial relations, postures, inferred states) are either directly visible or conservatively inferred from unambiguous visual cues — and ONLY applies when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation. The criterion does NOT penalize factual errors, hallucinations, or misidentifications — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It is a downstream refinement for factually correct answers only — not a tiebreaker or primary filter. When evaluating, annotators must: (a) confirm factual consistency and visual grounding first — if violated, multimodal_coherence is irrelevant; (b) check for internal contradictions (e.g., ‘standing on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path); (c) verify that inferred actions or states are grounded in observable posture, motion, or context (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ is inferable from posture, but ‘browsing Apple web pages’ is hallucinated unless Apple logos are visible); (d) penalize unsupported speculation — even if plausible — and reward only conservative, visually supported inferences. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Multimodal_coherence does not evaluate linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or aesthetic judgment — only strict fidelity to the visual record. It is not a tiebreaker for hallucinated or denied elements — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. Visual confirmation is sufficient when an object is clearly identifiable — even if its exact type is not — and should not penalize accurate descriptions of visible objects that are not perfectly certain in their type. ‘Conservative inference’ applies only when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — not when it is present but not fully clear. Descriptions of visible elements (even stylized or abstract) are not hallucinations if they are factually consistent — and should be reported without penalty. Spatial relationships like ‘beneath’ or ‘under’ are not hallucinations if they are visually supported by the image’s perspective — even if not immediately obvious. Non-living or static objects (e.g., statues) may be described with posture descriptions (e.g., ‘bent legs’) as long as they are visually grounded — regardless of biological plausibility. ‘Pattern’ is not a hallucination if it accurately describes a human image — and should not be penalized unless misrepresented (e.g., a photo misidentified as a ‘logo’ or ‘symbol’ without visual support). Color variations that are visually supported (e.g., ‘green’, ‘turquoise’, ‘blue-green’) are not hallucinations — and should not be penalized. Text labels within the image are part of the visual evidence — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. Hallucinations are only penalized when the claim contradicts verifiable visual evidence — not when the answer adds detail. ‘Unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details. ‘Conservative inference’ is not a justification for omitting visible elements — only for handling ambiguity. Visual evidence includes pixels, clear outlines, distinguishable symbols — and annotators must verify presence before applying ‘conservative inference’. The criterion must not penalize accurate but more detailed descriptions when they are visually supported. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether banana is ‘at the bottom’), a descriptive, non-inferential answer is preferred over speculative reconstruction — but only if the ambiguity is not resolved by other visual cues. The criterion should not penalize plausible explanations for why certain elements are missing — only hallucinations or misrepresentations — and should not be applied to answers that are factually inconsistent with the image. When in doubt, the answer that minimizes speculation and maximizes visual fidelity wins — but only if both are factually consistent. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, complete, or vague — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions. Additionally, the criterion must explicitly state that it is not applicable to hallucinated or misidentified elements — even if they are 'conservatively inferred' — because those elements are not factually consistent. It must also explicitly warn that attempting to apply multimodal_coherence to factually incorrect answers is an error — and that the worker should always first check factual consistency before evaluating multimodal_coherence. The description should emphasize that multimodal_coherence is a refinement for factually correct answers — not a tool to resolve ties between factually incorrect answers. It must explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is inapplicable to answers that are factually inconsistent — and that such answers should be disqualified at the factual_consistency_with_the_image stage. The criterion should clarify that it only penalizes visual misrepresentations or contradictions — not semantic or linguistic missteps that do not violate the visual record. It must also explicitly state that multimodal_coherence is only applicable to factually consistent and visually grounded answers — and that any answer with factual errors is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation, regardless of its internal consistency. The description should explicitly warn against using multimodal_coherence to evaluate or compare factually inconsistent answers — and must emphasize that it is only for refining comparisons among factually consistent answers. Finally, the criterion must explicitly clarify that emotional or behavioral inferences (like ‘joyously’) are not hallucinations if they are visually supported — and should not be penalized as ‘unsupported speculation’. It must also explicitly state that aesthetic judgments (like ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’) are not penalized under multimodal_coherence — and that ‘conservative inference’ does not mean avoiding subjective or emotional language — only avoiding unsupported claims. Additionally, the criterion should explicitly prohibit penalizing visually supported emotional or behavioral inferences for being ‘subjective’ — and must not confuse aesthetic language with hallucination. The criterion should also clarify that ‘conservative inference’ applies only to ambiguous visual cues — not to clear, observable behaviors — and must not penalize accurate emotional descriptions when they are visually grounded. Finally, it should explicitly state that multimodal_coherence does not evaluate aesthetic or emotional language — only visual fidelity — and that such language is not penalized unless it is hallucinated or misrepresents visual evidence.

current_criteria.name: specificity
current_criteria.description: Specificity evaluates the granularity and precision of visually verifiable details in an answer — including object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual elements — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation entirely, and no comparison should be made under this criterion. Specificity rewards answers that add accurate, non-hallucinated, granular details — even minor or non-essential ones — as long as they are visually verifiable and do not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral or environmental inferences (e.g., ‘waiting for their turn’ from posture, ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. However, it DOES penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’, ‘mirror effect’) that lacks visual grounding — as these are subjective and not descriptive of visual elements. Specificity does not reward speculative inferences — but does reward inclusion of verifiable, granular details like ‘a browser window’ — even if the action (e.g., ‘browsing’) is inferred. Hallucinations (fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible) are always penalized — even if highly detailed — and disqualify the answer from specificity evaluation. Specificity is not a tiebreaker — it applies only to factually consistent and visually grounded answers, and preference must be determined using foundational criteria (visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image) first. It is not about linguistic creativity or detail quantity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present and factually correct. Annotators should prioritize accurate, granular descriptions over vague or generic ones — but only if they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity must not override or compensate for violations of visual grounding or factual consistency — granularity is irrelevant if the answer is hallucinated or misrepresents the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative detail — and specificity is not applicable. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized — it is a hallucination. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if not central. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity is evaluated only after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is never applied to hallucinated or factually inconsistent answers. Additionally, specificity does not apply to artistic, abstract, or stylized visual elements — such as ‘pattern design’, ‘arc’, or ‘composition’ — unless they are visually verifiable or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues. Descriptive aesthetic terms (e.g., ‘eye-catching’) are only allowed if they are visually grounded — and must not be penalized for being non-essential. Contextually grounded inferences are rewarded if visually supported — even if not explicitly visible — as long as they are plausible and not hallucinated. Specificity is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded answers — and such answers must be disqualified from the entire preference comparison before any criterion evaluation. Finally, specificity rewards the most accurate, visually verifiable description — not the most semantically labeled one — and penalizes any answer that uses a semantic label (e.g., ‘logo’) that is not visually verifiable — while rewarding the answer that provides the most precise visual description — even if it uses descriptive terms (e.g., ‘human-shaped pattern’).

current_criteria.name: visual_grounding
current_criteria.description: Visual grounding evaluates whether every factual claim in the answer strictly corresponds to what is visibly present in the image — including object identity, spatial relationships, actions, colors, textures, structural support, and quantifiable features — without fabricating, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against the visual record using direct observation or conservative inference from unambiguous visual cues — not mental reconstruction, speculation, or external knowledge. Hallucinations — defined as fabricating non-existent visual elements, actions, relationships, or attributes — are always penalized, regardless of aesthetic appeal or contextual plausibility. Misrepresentations — such as misidentifying visible elements (e.g., mistaking a ceiling light for a TV) — are penalized only if they misrepresent the visual record; misidentifications of color or texture (e.g., ‘red’ vs. ‘orange’) are not hallucinations if the element is visibly present. Omission of clearly visible elements is penalized only if the element is semantically essential to answering the question or if its omission contradicts the visual record — otherwise, omission is not a violation. Contextually supported inferences (e.g., inferring ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window or ‘on shelves’ from visible shelf structure) are acceptable and not penalized, as long as they are grounded in direct visual cues and do not fabricate non-existent elements. Descriptive phrases like ‘mixed together’ or ‘small portion’ are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual scene — even if not perfectly uniform — as long as they are grounded in the visual record. Visual grounding does not penalize accurate, conservative, or relative descriptions of size and position — even if they differ from more absolute claims — as long as they are visually supported. It does not penalize accurate descriptions of visible postures (e.g., ‘legs bent’) — even if non-standard — or emotional/behavioral inferences (e.g., ‘smiling’, ‘browsing’) — as long as they are visually grounded and contextually plausible. Aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘eye-catching’, ‘balanced’) is not penalized — even if subjective — as long as it does not imply hallucinated visual attributes. Calibrated uncertainty (e.g., ‘possibly a tent’, ‘appears to be’) is rewarded for ambiguous visual elements — not penalized — and must be used instead of omission. The criterion applies only to factual, observable visual elements — not to subjective, aesthetic, or interpretive judgments — which are evaluated under other criteria. It is evaluated only after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. Visual grounding does not penalize overestimation of counts (e.g., ‘at least twelve’) if the number is visually supported — only if the claim exceeds visible evidence. It does not require pixel-perfect spatial precision — only contextually accurate spatial relationships (e.g., ‘in front of’, ‘behind’, ‘scattered’) — and penalizes only when misrepresentations are visually evident. Composite surfaces (e.g., whiteboards, canvases) and attached items (e.g., sticky notes) must be counted as distinct visual elements. Common or colloquial terms (e.g., ‘water scooter’ for jet ski) are acceptable if they do not misrepresent the object’s core visual identity — and are not hallucinations. Structural context (e.g., walls, floors, rods, shelves) must be described accurately — even if not central to the question — as they are critical visual elements. Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. The criterion must not be conflated with factual consistency or specificity — grounding is about fidelity to visual presence, not accuracy of interpretation. When visual evidence is ambiguous, the answer must reflect the ambiguity, not invent or omit. The criterion is always evaluated after confirming factual consistency — but only applies to factual, observable visual elements. If an answer contains hallucinations or misrepresents visible elements, it is automatically disqualified from visual grounding evaluation — regardless of other criteria. Visual grounding does not penalize for plausible inferences, minor misidentifications, or stylized depictions — unless they misrepresent or omit clearly visible elements. The criterion is inapplicable to non-living, stylized, or artistic representations unless their visual form is being misrepresented — and does not penalize descriptions of their pose or structure if they are visually present. Visual grounding is not applicable to non-visual elements — such as titles, artist attribution, or stylistic labels — which are evaluated under factual_consistency_with_the_image. The goal is to reward answers that reflect all visually present elements with precision — even if minor or ambiguous — and penalize only hallucinations and omissions of critical visual elements — not contextually accurate or inferential descriptions that are visually grounded.

current_criteria.name: visual_stability_and_motion_consistency
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description of motion, posture, or physical stability is consistent with visually evident cues of motion or stillness — such as motion blur, dynamic posture, implied movement, or static positioning — but ONLY when the question explicitly or implicitly involves motion, implied action, or dynamic scenes (e.g., ‘What is happening?’, ‘Is this person moving?’, ‘Describe the action’). It is inapplicable to static, non-motion-related questions (e.g., object identification, spatial arrangement, background description, or aesthetic judgments) — and must not be used to override or substitute for visual_grounding or factual_consistency_with_the_image. When applicable, it penalizes only contradictions between textual claims and visual evidence — e.g., describing a person as ‘running’ when no motion blur or dynamic posture is visible, or describing a static object as ‘in motion’ — but does NOT penalize accurate descriptions of implied motion (e.g., ‘leaning forward’ from posture) or static postures that are visually accurate. It does not evaluate the accuracy of motion type (e.g., ‘running’ vs. ‘walking’), nor does it penalize factual errors in object identity, color, or structure — those are handled under visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It also does NOT penalize stylistic, compositional, or contextual descriptors (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘unstructured’, ‘warehouse’) unless they imply motion or physical instability — and must not be conflated with physical motion or stability. The criterion is evaluated ONLY after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency — and if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from evaluation under this criterion. It is not a tiebreaker — and if the question is static or non-motion-related, the criterion is inapplicable and should not be used to compare answers. Annotators must report ‘inapplicable’ if motion/stability is not relevant to the question — and must defer to other criteria (e.g., visual_grounding, factual_consistency_with_the_image, semantic_alignment_with_question_intent) for static scenes. The criterion is strictly for motion/stability claims — not posture, seating, facial expressions, or emotional states — which are evaluated under other criteria. Visual evidence must be directly confirmed (e.g., motion blur, posture, spatial arrangement) — and descriptions must not infer motion or instability from ambiguous or non-visual cues (e.g., ‘no stop sign’ or ‘open space’). Descriptions of static posture (e.g., ‘standing’, ‘crouching’, ‘half-squatting’) are always compliant if visually supported — even if the scene implies potential motion — and should not be penalized unless contradicted by clear visual cues of motion. If both answers are static and factually consistent, preference should be determined by other criteria — not by motion/stability. The criterion must never be used to penalize descriptive accuracy, stylistic preference, or factual errors — only to flag contradictions between visual evidence and motion/stability claims. It must not be applied to stylized, symbolic, or artistic representations of action — unless the visual cues clearly depict physical motion (e.g., motion blur, posture). The goal is to ensure that motion or stability descriptions are grounded in visual evidence — not in plausible but unsupported inferences — and to avoid misapplication to static or non-motion questions.

current_criteria.name: temporal_coherence_of_visual_sequence
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s description of actions or states is consistent with the implied temporal sequence or progression in the image — especially in dynamic scenes (e.g., motion blur, overlapping objects, sequential actions). It applies only when the image contains visual cues suggesting temporal order (e.g., a person mid-stride, objects in motion, overlapping frames). It penalizes claims that violate implied temporal causality (e.g., describing a person as ‘just finished running’ when motion blur suggests ongoing motion). It rewards answers that respect visual sequencing — such as describing actions in a plausible temporal order — without assuming external context. It is evaluated after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and does not apply to static images or questions not involving implied motion or sequence. It does not penalize interpretive or aesthetic judgments — only factual claims about temporal order. It is not a tiebreaker — only applicable when temporal sequence matters. This criterion is distinct from ‘visual_stability_and_motion_consistency’ because it focuses on implied sequence — not physical stability. It is also distinct from ‘multimodal_coherence’ because it focuses on temporal alignment — not structural or semantic fidelity.

current_criteria.name: language_precision_and_grammatical_fidelity
current_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer’s language is precise, grammatically correct, and minimally ambiguous — avoiding vague terms, ungrammatical structures, or ambiguous pronouns — while preserving semantic clarity. It applies to all answers — regardless of visual complexity — and is evaluated after verifying visual grounding and factual consistency. It penalizes language that is overly verbose, stylistically redundant, or grammatically incorrect — but does not penalize stylistic or interpretive language if it is clear and unambiguous. It rewards answers that use precise, grammatically correct language — even if the content is factually consistent — to enhance clarity and reduce misinterpretation. It is not a tiebreaker — only applicable when language clarity is ambiguous or when answers are factually consistent but linguistically divergent. It does not evaluate the accuracy of visual content — only the linguistic precision. For example: ‘The person is holding a red cup’ is preferred over ‘The person has a cup, and it’s red’ — if both are factually consistent — for grammatical concision. It also penalizes ambiguous pronouns (e.g., ‘it’ without clear antecedent) — even if visually grounded. This criterion is distinct from ‘clear_language’ (which is being removed) because it focuses on grammatical and lexical precision — not general clarity. It is also distinct from ‘specificity’ because it focuses on linguistic form — not visual granularity. It does not apply to aesthetic or subjective interpretations — which are evaluated under other criteria.

all_criteria.name: visual_grounding
all_criteria.description: The answer must strictly and precisely reflect only what is visually present in the image — including object identity, location, spatial relationships, actions, colors, shapes, and quantifiable features — without inventing, omitting, or misrepresenting visible elements. Annotators must verify each claim against direct visual evidence: if an object is visible, it must be named correctly and positioned accurately; if an object is absent, it must not be claimed to be present. Visual grounding requires fidelity to observable details, including subtle or partially obscured elements (e.g., numbers, logos, textures), and penalizes both hallucinations (adding non-existent details) and false omissions (omitting visible elements that mislead or contradict the image’s content). It does not require minimalism or abstraction — detailed, accurate descriptions are preferred if they are visually supported. Annotators should avoid speculative inferences or structural assumptions not directly visible (e.g., inferring motion or implied structure without visual cues), and should flag uncertainty when visual evidence is ambiguous. The criterion is inapplicable only when the question asks for opinion, interpretation, or subjective judgment — otherwise, visual grounding is always evaluated. Examples: ‘A red car parked on the left’ is grounded; ‘A red car parked’ is insufficient if the left/right is critical; ‘A red car with a black roof’ is grounded if the roof is visible; ‘A red car with a black object on top’ is hallucinated if no such object exists.

all_criteria.name: factual_consistency_with_the_image
all_criteria.description: The answer must align precisely with the visually verifiable elements present in the image — no fabrication, misidentification, omission of clearly visible elements, or misrepresentation of spatial, structural, or visual attributes is permitted. Annotators evaluate whether every claimed visual detail (objects, positions, colors, textures, labels, spatial relationships, and micro-details) is directly supported by what is visibly present. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., blurry text, partially obscured objects), the answer may express calibrated uncertainty (e.g., 'possibly 5 pillows') — but must not fabricate or omit elements that are clearly visible. Omitting visible elements is a factual inconsistency unless those elements are explicitly irrelevant to the question. The criterion applies only to observable, static, geometric, or structural visual cues — motion blur, implied motion, or contextual inferences (e.g., 'warehouse from shelves') are not grounds for factual inconsistency if they do not contradict visible structure. Hallucinations include adding nonexistent objects, misidentifying existing ones, or claiming actions not visually supported — even if plausible. Factual consistency does not require pixel-perfect accuracy or exhaustive detail — only that claims match the visual record. Subjective inferences (e.g., 'calm,' 'arrogant') or aesthetic judgments are not hallucinations unless they imply a fabricated visual attribute. Contextual or inferential claims are permitted if visually plausible and do not contradict the image. The criterion does not apply to questions asking for opinions, interpretations, or non-visual metadata (e.g., artist names, titles). When two answers are factually consistent, tiebreakers are applied based on completeness or specificity — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge, and must reject any claim that contradicts the visual record, even if it seems 'reasonable.' Additionally, the criterion explicitly clarifies: (1) Denying the presence of an object is factually consistent if that object is not visually present; omitting other visible objects is not a factual inconsistency unless those objects are directly relevant to answering the question; (2) Factual consistency is evaluated for each specific claim — not for completeness of the entire scene — and hallucinations (misidentifications) are penalized even if other elements are omitted or inaccurately described; (3) Subjective interpretations of visual arrangement (e.g., 'chaotic spacing', 'orderly formation') are permitted as long as they do not contradict the visible structure — and are not penalized as factual inconsistencies; (4) Factual consistency does not penalize detail accuracy or completeness — only hallucinations, misidentifications, or omissions of clearly visible elements; (5) Visible elements, even if minor or non-central, are essential to factual consistency — and omitting them (especially if they are directly observable) constitutes a factual inconsistency; (6) Factual consistency applies only to visual elements — not titles, artist names, or metadata — and visual elements must be confirmed against the image, not external knowledge; (7) Subjective or stylistic visual attributes (like 'red cheeks') are not hallucinations if they are visually supported; (8) 'Factual consistency' does not apply to non-visual elements — which are evaluated under other criteria — to avoid confusion and misapplication; (9) Relative size or spatial descriptors (e.g., 'small portion,' 'most of the space') are acceptable as long as they are visually accurate — and 'small' does not imply hallucination if the object occupies a portion of the frame; (10) Structural or spatial claims (e.g., 'on shelves' vs. 'hanging from ceiling') must be visually verifiable — and any inference contradicting clear visual structure is a factual inconsistency; (11) Factual consistency requires accurate description of individual visual states when multiple subjects or varying conditions exist — not overgeneralization; (12) Answers must match the specific term requested in the question (e.g., 'English language term'), even if a different term is visually accurate or commonly used — but functional or contextual descriptions are allowed if they are non-visual and non-hallucinated; (13) Factual consistency requires reporting all clearly visible elements — not just avoiding fabrication — and 'unclear' only applies to ambiguous visual cues, not to cases where elements are clearly present but miscounted or misidentified; (14) Omitting visible elements — even if the worker is unsure about their role — is a factual inconsistency, and the number of visible elements must be accurately reported unless explicitly ambiguous (e.g., 'blurry', 'partially obscured'); (15) Adding non-essential, accurate details (e.g., background color, posture, facial expression) is acceptable and does not constitute factual inconsistency; (16) Hallucinations include not only adding nonexistent objects but also misidentifying or misrepresenting visible elements — such as claiming an object is 'revealing his upper body' when the visual evidence shows he is wearing a shirt; (17) Descriptions of visual elements that are inherently stylized, symbolic, or graphic — including implied motion or action — are acceptable as long as they are not hallucinations; (18) Factual consistency does not penalize accurate, non-hallucinated details — even if they are non-essential or redundant — as long as they are visually supported; (19) The criterion explicitly distinguishes between visually verifiable elements and inferred context — penalizing only when inferred claims contradict visual evidence — and must clarify that calibrated uncertainty should not be used to justify unsupported inferences; (20) Factual consistency does not prohibit reasonable, non-hallucinated inferences about behavior, threat, or context — as long as they are grounded in the visible subject’s state and do not fabricate or misrepresent visual elements; (21) The criterion must be revised to clarify that 'factual consistency' applies only to observable, structural, or geometric visual cues — not to abstract or interpretive descriptions — and that aesthetic or compositional terms (e.g., 'scattered', 'concentrated') are acceptable if they accurately reflect the visual evidence; (22) Labeled text within the image is considered part of the visual record and must be respected — and factual consistency requires matching claims to all visual cues — including labels, even if they are stylized or child-like — and not just to visual objects or structure; (23) The absence of a label does not imply a claim is hallucinated — and labeled elements must be verified as visually present, not inferred or imagined; (24) If an element is labeled in the image, its description must be factually consistent — even if the label is ambiguous or artistic — and that labels should not be ignored or overruled by other visual cues unless the label contradicts the visual record.

all_criteria.name: avoidance_of_hallucinated_visual_details
all_criteria.description: The answer must not invent or exaggerate visual details not present in the image. For example, claiming a person is holding a phone when none is visible, or describing a background object that doesn’t exist — such details are considered hallucinations and reduce quality.

all_criteria.name: question_relevance
all_criteria.description: The answer must directly address the question asked. If the question asks about composition, an answer focusing on the animal’s mood is off-topic. Annotators check whether the answer targets the core intent of the question, not tangential or irrelevant information.

all_criteria.name: completeness
all_criteria.description: Completeness is evaluated ONLY for answers that are factually consistent with the image and visually grounded — any answer containing hallucinations, misidentifications, or direct visual contradictions is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation, regardless of detail level. Completeness measures whether the answer includes all visually present elements that are semantically required to fully answer the question’s literal intent — defined as elements directly necessary to satisfy the question’s core factual demand (e.g., object identity, spatial relationships, posture, motion, or contextually grounded actions). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — if either is violated, completeness is inapplicable. If an answer is factually consistent, completeness is judged by whether it covers all semantically essential visual components — not all visible details, nor aesthetic descriptors, nor speculative inferences — and omission of clearly visible, semantically essential elements (e.g., posture when asked ‘what is the person doing?’) is penalized. Adding non-essential, hallucinated, or contextually unsupported details (e.g., ‘a camel’ not visible) does not improve completeness — it reduces quality. Completeness does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or stylistic descriptions (e.g., ‘messy’, ‘balanced’) unless they are visually grounded and semantically relevant to answering the question — and even then, they are not required. Completeness is not about verbosity or exhaustive listing — it is about covering only the essential visual components required to fully answer the question’s literal intent. If two answers are factually consistent, the one that includes more semantically essential, visually present elements wins — but only if those elements are not hallucinated. Completeness is never used to override factual consistency — factual consistency is the non-negotiable prerequisite. If an answer is factually inconsistent, it cannot be considered complete, regardless of its detail level. Completeness is evaluated only after factual consistency is confirmed — and only among factually consistent answers. Annotators must reject any answer that contains factual errors for completeness evaluation, and instead evaluate it based on factual consistency first. The criterion does not apply to open-ended, interpretive, or aesthetic questions — in which case, visual grounding and factual consistency are the only evaluation criteria. Completeness should not be used to penalize accurate but non-critical details — e.g., background colors or subtle textures — unless they are essential to answering the question’s intent. If the question does not require object identification or description, then object details are not essential — and omitting them does not constitute incompleteness. The goal is to ensure that factually correct answers are complete in their coverage of the question’s core intent, without over-rewarding detail or penalizing accurate but peripheral descriptions. Examples: For ‘What is the person doing?’, ‘standing’ is essential; ‘wearing a red shirt’ is non-essential unless the question asks about clothing. For ‘What is in the foreground?’, omitting a visible object is incomplete; for ‘What is the object?’, omitting visible shape or color is incomplete if those are essential to identification. Completeness does not reward speculative or non-visual inferences — e.g., ‘in a warehouse’ is allowed if visually supported, but ‘has a secret code’ is hallucinated and disqualifies the answer. Annotators must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge or cultural assumptions — and must not penalize for minor factual errors (e.g., color misidentification) if the core object or action is correctly described and visually grounded. Completeness is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent answers — but it should not be used to penalize minor factual errors that do not undermine the overall factual consistency or visual grounding. Finally, completeness does not apply to questions where the context is not visually relevant (e.g., team identification, jersey norms) unless explicitly required by the question’s intent. The criterion must explicitly define 'semantically essential' as elements required by the question’s literal intent — not architectural or structural features — and must clarify that contextual, non-essential details (like a Coca-Cola box) are still 'complete' if visually present, and that omitting such elements does not constitute incompleteness unless they are directly relevant to answering the question. It must also explicitly exclude architectural elements from being considered 'essential' unless the question is about room structure or layout. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only evaluated for factually consistent answers — and that if both candidates are factually inconsistent, neither is eligible for completeness evaluation — and preference must be determined by other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). It must also clarify that a factual error (like misidentifying color) disqualifies an answer from completeness evaluation, regardless of how well it describes other visible elements. Additionally, the criterion should specify that if one answer is factually consistent and the other is not, the consistent one should be preferred — but if both are factually inconsistent, completeness is not applicable and the worker must rely on other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, clarity, or plausibility). The criterion must explicitly state that completeness is only applicable when the question’s literal intent requires specific visual elements beyond simple count or identification — e.g., spatial arrangement, functional use, or configuration — and must not penalize omissions of non-essential details (like spatial distribution) when the core factual requirement (e.g., count) is satisfied. It must also explicitly state that 'semantically essential' elements are defined only within the context of factually correct answers — and that any claim that is factually wrong (even if more specific) is automatically disqualified from completeness evaluation. The criterion must explicitly prohibit rewarding speculative or contextually inferred arrangements that are not visually supported — even if they seem ‘semantically essential’. It must clarify that completeness only applies to literal, factual descriptions — not interpretive or inferred structures — and must penalize any answer that misrepresents the visual arrangement, even if it seems plausible. The criterion should also specify that ‘semantically essential’ elements must be visually present or conservatively inferred from unambiguous cues — not speculative reconstruction — and must not reward hallucinated structures even if they seem ‘logical’ or ‘contextually appropriate’. Finally, it should clarify that completeness does not apply to questions asking for ‘how’ or ‘why’ — which might imply interpretation — and must be strictly applied to literal, factual descriptions. The criterion must explicitly state that 'semantically required' elements are defined by the question’s literal intent, not by contextual or interpretive assumptions. It must also clarify that adding non-essential, visually present details is not a strength under completeness — and that factual consistency is a non-negotiable prerequisite. Furthermore, the criterion should warn annotators that 'semantically required' does not mean 'contextually relevant' or 'socially appropriate' — and that visual presence alone is insufficient if the element is not required by the question. Finally, the criterion must explicitly forbid using completeness to override factual consistency — and must clarify that if one answer is hallucinated, it is disqualified from completeness evaluation regardless of detail level. The criterion must explicitly state that completeness rewards inclusion of all visually present, semantically essential elements — not omitting them for stylistic or aesthetic reasons. It must clarify that 'essential' means necessary for answering the question's literal intent — not minimal or concise. The description should penalize omission of visually present elements unless they are irrelevant to the question — and must explicitly forbid penalizing accurate, visually grounded details for being 'non-essential' or 'non-critical' unless they are genuinely irrelevant. The criterion should also clarify that 'completeness' is not about conciseness or accuracy of terminology — only about covering the visually necessary elements. Finally, it should explicitly warn against penalizing answers for including visually present, semantically relevant details that are not required for literal accuracy — even if they are not the most 'precise' or 'concise'.

all_criteria.name: specificity
all_criteria.description: Specificity measures the granularity and precision with which an answer describes visually verifiable elements in the image — including object type, color, texture, spatial position, configuration, brand names, labels, or contextual details — but ONLY when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from specificity evaluation. Specificity rewards answers that add verifiable, non-hallucinated details that enhance visual fidelity — even minor or non-essential elements — as long as they are accurately described and do not misrepresent scale, position, or proportion. It does NOT penalize contextually grounded behavioral or environmental inferences (e.g., ‘waiting for their turn’ from posture, ‘browsing’ from a visible browser window) — as long as they are visually supported and not hallucinated. However, it DOES penalize aesthetic or interpretive language (e.g., ‘eye-catching’, ‘visually appealing’) that lacks visual grounding — as these are not descriptive of visual elements but subjective judgments. Specificity does not reward speculative inferences — but does reward inclusion of verifiable, granular details like ‘a browser window’ — even if the action (e.g., ‘browsing’) is inferred. Hallucinations (fabricated objects, actions, or attributes not visible) are always penalized — even if highly detailed — and disqualify the answer from specificity evaluation. Specificity is not a tiebreaker for factually inconsistent or visually ungrounded answers — those are disqualified before any comparison. It is not about linguistic creativity or detail quantity — it is about precision in describing what is visually present and factually correct. Annotators should prioritize accurate, granular descriptions over vague or generic ones — but only if they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity must not override or compensate for violations of visual grounding or factual consistency — granularity is irrelevant if the answer is hallucinated or misrepresents the visual record. When visual evidence is ambiguous, calibrated uncertainty should be used — not speculative detail — and specificity is not applicable. Examples: ‘a red sedan with a sunroof parked next to a curb’ is more specific than ‘a red sedan parked’ — both are grounded and factually consistent. ‘A cat with a golden collar’ is penalized — it is a hallucination. ‘A person holding hands with a child’ is rewarded — if the child is visually present. ‘A person with an angry expression’ is penalized — if ‘angry’ is not visually verifiable. ‘A person with a red jacket’ is rewarded — if the jacket is visible. ‘A person with a red jacket that is eye-catching’ is penalized — ‘eye-catching’ is aesthetic and not visually verifiable. ‘A person browsing a web page’ is not penalized — if a browser window is visible — but ‘a person browsing a web page on a laptop’ is rewarded — if the laptop is visible. ‘A person waiting for their turn’ is penalized — if not visually implied — even if plausible. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt’ is rewarded — if the logo is visible — even if not central. ‘A person with a logo on their shirt that says ‘Nike’’ is rewarded — if the text is visible — even if not central. Specificity must not be used to evaluate or override factual consistency — if one answer is factually incorrect, it is always inferior, regardless of specificity. Specificity is not a substitute for accuracy — any factual error or hallucination automatically disqualifies the answer. It is only applicable for factual, visually grounded answers — and does not apply to aesthetic, subjective, or non-visual judgments — unless grounded in observable visual cues. The goal is to reward answers that add precision and granularity to the description of visually present elements — without introducing hallucinations or misrepresenting the visual record. Annotators should prioritize verifiable, granular details — even if minor or non-essential — over vague or generic descriptions — as long as they remain factually consistent and visually grounded. Specificity is evaluated only after factual consistency and visual grounding are confirmed — and is never applied to hallucinated or factually inconsistent answers.

all_criteria.name: calibrated_uncertainty
all_criteria.description: The answer should reflect confidence appropriately. If the image is ambiguous, the answer should indicate uncertainty (e.g., “possibly” or “likely”) without overstating certainty. Annotators penalize overconfidence in uncertain situations and reward humility when appropriate.

all_criteria.name: clear_language
all_criteria.description: The answer should be written in simple, grammatically correct, and unambiguous language. Jargon, overly complex phrasing, or unclear syntax reduce clarity and accessibility. Annotators prefer answers that are easy to understand without requiring interpretation.

all_criteria.name: logical_consistency
all_criteria.description: The answer must be internally coherent and free from contradictions. For example, if it says an animal is both “calm” and “in pain,” or that objects are “on opposite sides” while also “centered,” it lacks logical consistency. Annotators evaluate whether the answer’s internal logic aligns with the visual evidence.

all_criteria.name: biological_or_contextual_plausibility
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether an answer’s description of living beings (humans, animals) or their contextual interactions is contextually reasonable and grounded in the visual evidence — but ONLY after the answer has been confirmed to be factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. It does NOT apply to non-living subjects (e.g., statues, logos, abstract art, objects), abstract representations, or spatial arrangements unless they imply biological or physical impossibility (e.g., a giraffe in a cage). Annotators must first verify visual grounding and factual consistency — any violation automatically disqualifies the answer from plausibility evaluation. Plausibility is not a tiebreaker or secondary filter — it is strictly a post-verification assessment used to resolve ties between factually consistent, visually grounded answers. It must be based solely on observable visual cues and real-world biological/physical plausibility — no speculation, external knowledge, or aesthetic judgment is permitted. Examples: ‘A dog lying down’ is plausible; ‘A dog singing opera’ is implausible. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., indistinct posture), the answer should remain neutral or descriptive — plausibility judgments are not made. Plausibility rewards interpretations that are contextually reasonable and visually supported — even if detailed — and does not penalize specificity or detail as long as they are grounded. It explicitly excludes evaluative or interpretive claims (e.g., ‘calm,’ ‘arrogant’) unless directly supported by visual cues (e.g., relaxed posture). When in doubt, prefer the answer that makes the fewest speculative assumptions while remaining factually grounded. Plausibility is inapplicable for non-living subjects — such answers are evaluated under other criteria (e.g., visual grounding, factual consistency). If the criterion is inapplicable, preference must be determined by other applicable criteria — not by defaulting to caution or omitting details. Annotators must never use plausibility to justify hallucinations, misidentifications, or unsupported inferences — these are penalized under visual grounding and factual consistency. Directional or spatial qualifiers (e.g., ‘toward the left’, ‘extended forward’) are allowed if visually supported — they are not speculative if grounded. Plausibility is not a tool to reward minimalism or penalize contextual detail — it is strictly for rejecting falsehoods in behavior or context. When visual evidence supports an emotional or behavioral inference (e.g., open mouth, raised arms), such terms are not speculative — they are valid under plausibility. Plausibility is not a substitute for visual grounding or factual consistency — if either is violated, the answer is disqualified regardless of plausibility. The criterion is strictly for inferred behavior, not event type or setting — any suggestion of a setting (e.g., ‘stage’, ‘competition’) that contradicts the visual context is a violation. It does not apply to social norms or cultural expectations unless directly supported by visual evidence. Plausibility is never applied to neutral or descriptive observations (e.g., ‘standing with legs apart’) — such observations are always preferred over speculative inferences. The criterion must never be used to evaluate symbolic, stylized, or thematic interpretations (e.g., ‘train-themed’) — these are evaluated under other criteria. Annotators must reject any answer that introduces or misrepresents non-visual or fabricated elements — even if plausible — and must prioritize visual evidence over external knowledge. Plausibility is evaluated only after visual grounding and factual consistency are confirmed — and only among answers that meet those prerequisites. If two answers are equally grounded and consistent, plausibility is used to resolve the tie — but only if both are factually correct. Hallucinations (even if plausible) are always penalized — and plausibility is never a tiebreaker if one answer is factually incorrect. The criterion is inapplicable for non-living subjects — and such answers are evaluated under other criteria. If an answer is factually incorrect or visually unsupported, plausibility evaluation is irrelevant — the answer is disqualified. The goal is to ensure that plausibility judgments are contextually reasonable, visually grounded, and do not override factual consistency or visual grounding. Annotators must avoid conflating plausibility with speculation — and must only evaluate it for grounded, factual descriptions of living beings or their actions. Plausibility is not a preference rule — it is a verification filter for contextual reasonableness in living beings only.

all_criteria.name: multimodal_coherence
all_criteria.description: Multimodal_coherence evaluates the internal consistency and visual fidelity of an answer’s claims — specifically, whether all stated visual elements (objects, actions, spatial relations, postures, inferred states) are either directly visible or conservatively inferred from unambiguous visual cues — and ONLY applies when the answer is factually consistent with the image and visually grounded. Annotators must first verify factual consistency and visual grounding: if either is violated, the answer is disqualified from multimodal_coherence evaluation. The criterion does NOT penalize factual errors, hallucinations, or misidentifications — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. It is a downstream refinement for factually correct answers only — not a tiebreaker or primary filter. When evaluating, annotators must: (a) confirm factual consistency and visual grounding first — if violated, multimodal_coherence is irrelevant; (b) check for internal contradictions (e.g., ‘standing on a curved track’ while the image shows a straight path); (c) verify that inferred actions or states are grounded in observable posture, motion, or context (e.g., ‘drinking from a bowl’ is inferable from posture, but ‘browsing Apple web pages’ is hallucinated unless Apple logos are visible); (d) penalize unsupported speculation — even if plausible — and reward only conservative, visually supported inferences. If two answers are factually consistent, the one with fewer contradictions or more conservative inferences is preferred — but only after factual consistency is confirmed. Multimodal_coherence does not evaluate linguistic style, completeness, plausibility, or aesthetic judgment — only strict fidelity to the visual record. It is not a tiebreaker for hallucinated or denied elements — those are handled by visual_grounding and factual_consistency_with_the_image. Visual confirmation is sufficient when an object is clearly identifiable — even if its exact type is not — and should not penalize accurate descriptions of visible objects that are not perfectly certain in their type. ‘Conservative inference’ applies only when visual evidence is ambiguous or insufficient — not when it is present but not fully clear. Descriptions of visible elements (even stylized or abstract) are not hallucinations if they are factually consistent — and should be reported without penalty. Spatial relationships like ‘beneath’ or ‘under’ are not hallucinations if they are visually supported by the image’s perspective — even if not immediately obvious. Non-living or static objects (e.g., statues) may be described with posture descriptions (e.g., ‘bent legs’) as long as they are visually grounded — regardless of biological plausibility. ‘Pattern’ is not a hallucination if it accurately describes a human image — and should not be penalized unless misrepresented (e.g., a photo misidentified as a ‘logo’ or ‘symbol’ without visual support). Color variations that are visually supported (e.g., ‘green’, ‘turquoise’, ‘blue-green’) are not hallucinations — and should not be penalized. Text labels within the image are part of the visual evidence — and descriptive phrases matching labels are not hallucinations — they are rewarded. Hallucinations are only penalized when the claim contradicts verifiable visual evidence — not when the answer adds detail. ‘Unsupported speculation’ applies only to claims that misrepresent the image’s structure or content — not to accurate but non-essential details. ‘Conservative inference’ is not a justification for omitting visible elements — only for handling ambiguity. Visual evidence includes pixels, clear outlines, distinguishable symbols — and annotators must verify presence before applying ‘conservative inference’. The criterion must not penalize accurate but more detailed descriptions when they are visually supported. If visual evidence is ambiguous (e.g., whether banana is ‘at the bottom’), a descriptive, non-inferential answer is preferred over speculative reconstruction — but only if the ambiguity is not resolved by other visual cues. The criterion should not penalize plausible explanations for why certain elements are missing — only hallucinations or misrepresentations — and should not be applied to answers that are factually inconsistent with the image. When in doubt, the answer that minimizes speculation and maximizes visual fidelity wins — but only if both are factually consistent. The goal is to reward answers that are faithful to the visual record — not stylistically conservative, complete, or vague — and to penalize only hallucinations or contradictions.

all_criteria.name: cultural_or_situational_appropriateness
all_criteria.description: This criterion evaluates whether the answer avoids culturally inappropriate, socially insensitive, or contextually misleading interpretations — especially when the image contains cultural symbols, social contexts, or implicit social dynamics (e.g., gender roles, religious imagery, or regional stereotypes).
